items.stem: What are the standard conditions used for standard enthalpy changes?
items.answer: 298 K and 101 kPa
items.markingKey: Standard conditions: 298 K, 101 kPa, solutions 1.00 mol dm⁻³, substances in standard states.

items.stem: Explain why the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation for HCl and NaOH is the same as for HNO₃ and KOH.
items.answer: Both are strong acids and strong bases, fully ionised; the reaction in each case is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
items.markingKey: fully ionised [1]; same ionic equation [1]

items.stem: Explain why the enthalpy change of neutralisation of ethanoic acid with NaOH is less exothermic than that of HCl with NaOH.
items.answer: Ethanoic acid is weak and only partly ionised; some energy is used to ionise it as it reacts.
items.markingKey: weak acid partly ionised [1]; energy used for ionisation [1]

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +90 kJ mol⁻¹ and an activation energy of 120 kJ mol⁻¹. Sketch a labelled reaction pathway diagram and calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
items.answer: endothermic: products above reactants; Ea(reverse) = 30 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: products above reactants with ΔH labelled [1]; Ea hump labelled from reactants [1]; Ea(reverse) = 120 − (+90) = 30 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +206 kJ mol⁻¹ and an activation energy of 246 kJ mol⁻¹. Sketch a labelled reaction pathway diagram and calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
items.answer: endothermic: products above reactants; Ea(reverse) = 40 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: products above reactants with ΔH labelled [1]; Ea hump labelled from reactants [1]; Ea(reverse) = 246 − (+206) = 40 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Arjun is studying the combustion of hydrogen as a fuel for a project in Bangkok. (a) Define standard enthalpy change of combustion and write the equation for hydrogen. (b) Sketch a reaction pathway diagram for the combustion, labelling ΔH and Ea.
items.answer: (a) One mole burned completely in excess O₂ under standard conditions; H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) (b) Products below reactants; ΔH negative arrow down; Ea from reactants to peak.
items.markingKey: (a) One mole burned completely in excess O₂ under standard conditions; H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) [2] (b) Products below reactants; ΔH negative arrow down; Ea from reactants to peak. [2]

items.stem: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?
options: ΔH is positive and the surroundings cool
ΔH is negative and energy is transferred to the surroundings
ΔH is negative and the surroundings cool
items.answer: ΔH is negative and energy is transferred to the surroundings
items.markingKey: Exothermic: products lower in enthalpy than reactants; temperature of surroundings rises.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why a reaction is exothermic.
items.answer: More energy is released in forming the bonds in the products than is absorbed in breaking the bonds in the reactants.
items.markingKey: bond breaking endothermic, making exothermic [1]; energy released > absorbed [1]

items.stem: Explain why standard conditions must be stated for enthalpy changes.
items.answer: Enthalpy changes depend on temperature, pressure, concentration and physical states, so a reference is needed to compare values.
items.markingKey: ΔH depends on conditions/states [1]; allows comparison [1]

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +131 kJ mol⁻¹ and activation energy 251 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
items.answer: 120 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: Ea(reverse) = Ea − ΔH = 120 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹ and an activation energy of 120 kJ mol⁻¹. Sketch a labelled reaction pathway diagram and calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
items.answer: exothermic: products below reactants; Ea(reverse) = 212 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: products below reactants with ΔH labelled [1]; Ea hump labelled from reactants [1]; Ea(reverse) = 120 − (−92) = 212 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: A fuel company in Santiago reports enthalpy data for propane. (a) Sketch a reaction pathway diagram for the combustion, labelling ΔH and Ea. (b) Write the equation for the standard enthalpy change of formation of water.
items.answer: (a) Products below reactants; ΔH negative arrow down; Ea from reactants to peak. (b) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l)
items.markingKey: (a) Products below reactants; ΔH negative arrow down; Ea from reactants to peak. [2] (b) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) [1]

items.stem: Samuel is studying the combustion of methanol as a fuel for a project in Auckland. (a) Explain why combustion is exothermic in terms of bonds. (b) Explain why the fuel does not burn until it is ignited. (c) Write the equation for the standard enthalpy change of formation of water.
items.answer: (a) Energy released forming bonds in CO₂/H₂O exceeds energy absorbed breaking bonds in fuel and O₂. (b) The activation energy must be supplied to break bonds and start the reaction. (c) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l)
items.markingKey: (a) Energy released forming bonds in CO₂/H₂O exceeds energy absorbed breaking bonds in fuel and O₂. [2] (b) The activation energy must be supplied to break bonds and start the reaction. [1] (c) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) [1]

items.stem: In q = mcΔT, what does c represent?
options: the specific heat capacity of the liquid being heated
the heat capacity of the calorimeter only
items.answer: the specific heat capacity of the liquid being heated
items.markingKey: c of water/dilute solutions = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

items.stem: Explain why the experimental enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol is much less exothermic than the data-book value.
items.answer: Heat is lost to the surroundings (air, can); incomplete combustion; evaporation of fuel; non-standard conditions.
items.markingKey: heat loss [1]; one other valid reason [1]

items.stem: Suggest two improvements to a spirit-burner experiment to obtain a more accurate value of ΔHc.
items.answer: Use a draught shield/lid; insulate the can; use a copper calorimeter; keep the flame close; put a cap on the burner when weighing; stir the water.
items.markingKey: any two improvements [2]

items.stem: Samuel, a student in Santiago, burns 0.80 g of methanol, CH₃OH, in a spirit burner under a copper can containing 250 g of water. The temperature of the water rises by 8.7 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of methanol in kJ mol⁻¹. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
items.answer: −364 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Zara, a student in Bogotá, burns 0.60 g of heptane, C₇H₁₆, in a spirit burner under a copper can containing 200 g of water. The temperature of the water rises by 17.3 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of heptane in kJ mol⁻¹. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
items.answer: −2410 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Amara, a student in Kathmandu, burns 0.80 g of ethanol, C₂H₅OH, in a spirit burner under a copper can containing 100 g of water. The temperature of the water rises by 31.3 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol in kJ mol⁻¹. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹) The data-book value is -1367 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the percentage of the energy released that was transferred to the water and suggest one reason for the difference.
items.answer: −752 kJ mol⁻¹; 55.0%; heat lost to the surroundings

items.stem: Priya burns 0.80 g of propan-1-ol in a spirit burner to heat 200 g of water in a copper can. The temperature rises by 14.5 °C. (a) Calculate the energy transferred to the water. (b) Write the equation for the complete combustion, with state symbols. (c) The thermometer reads to ±0.5 °C. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature rise.
items.answer: (a) 12,100 J (b) C₃H₇OH(l) + ₄½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l) (c) 6.90%
items.markingKey: (a) 12,100 J [1] (b) C₃H₇OH(l) + ₄½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l) [2] (c) two readings: ±1.0 °C on ΔT [1]

items.stem: Arjun burns 0.80 g of methanol in a spirit burner to heat 200 g of water in a copper can. The temperature rises by 9.8 °C. (a) The data-book value is -726 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest two reasons for the difference. (b) Suggest two improvements to the experiment. (c) The thermometer reads to ±0.5 °C. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature rise.
items.answer: (a) Heat loss to surroundings; incomplete combustion; heat absorbed by can; evaporation of fuel. (b) Draught shield/insulation; lid; reduce distance from flame; weigh burner with cap on. (c) 10.2%
items.markingKey: (a) Heat loss to surroundings; incomplete combustion; heat absorbed by can; evaporation of fuel. [2] (b) Draught shield/insulation; lid; reduce distance from flame; weigh burner with cap on. [2] (c) two readings: ±1.0 °C on ΔT [1]

items.stem: Why is a polystyrene cup used as a calorimeter for reactions in solution?
options: it is a good thermal insulator with a low heat capacity
items.answer: it is a good thermal insulator with a low heat capacity
items.markingKey: Reduces heat loss to the surroundings.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Why is the temperature change extrapolated back to the time of mixing on a temperature–time graph? (b) What mass is used for m when 25.0 cm³ of acid is mixed with 25.0 cm³ of alkali?
items.answer: (a) to allow for heat lost while the reaction was taking place (b) 50.0 g
items.markingKey: (a) Extrapolation estimates the maximum temperature change if no heat were lost. (b) Assume density 1.00 g cm⁻³: total volume 50.0 cm³ → 50.0 g.

items.stem: Explain why the temperature rise is the same when 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl is neutralised by 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH as when 100 cm³ of each is used.
items.answer: Twice the amount of water forms, releasing twice the energy, but this heats twice the mass of solution, so ΔT is the same.
items.markingKey: energy doubles [1]; mass doubles, same ΔT [1]

items.stem: In a test answer, Mohammed states: "The enthalpy change is positive because the temperature of the water went up." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. A rise in temperature of the surroundings means the reaction is exothermic, so ΔH is negative.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Lina, a student in Madrid, mixes 40.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ nitric acid with 40.0 cm³ of 0.50 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 3.4 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation. Assume the solution has density 1.00 g cm⁻³ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
items.answer: −56.8 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Omar, a student in Karachi, burns 0.60 g of hexane, C₆H₁₄, in a spirit burner under a copper can containing 100 g of water. The temperature of the water rises by 41.7 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of hexane in kJ mol⁻¹. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
items.answer: −2500 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Mei, a student in Lagos, mixes 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid with 25.0 cm³ of 0.50 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 3.4 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation. Assume the solution has density 1.00 g cm⁻³ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
items.answer: −56.8 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: In a university teaching laboratory in Dhaka, students heat 200 g of water using 0.60 g of butan-1-ol. The water temperature increases by 11.7 °C. (a) Calculate the energy transferred to the water. (b) The data-book value is -2676 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest two reasons for the difference. (c) Suggest two improvements to the experiment.
items.answer: (a) 9780 J (b) Heat loss to surroundings; incomplete combustion; heat absorbed by can; evaporation of fuel. (c) Draught shield/insulation; lid; reduce distance from flame; weigh burner with cap on.
items.markingKey: (a) 9780 J [1] (b) Heat loss to surroundings; incomplete combustion; heat absorbed by can; evaporation of fuel. [2] (c) Draught shield/insulation; lid; reduce distance from flame; weigh burner with cap on. [2]

items.stem: Ines burns 0.90 g of propan-1-ol in a spirit burner to heat 200 g of water in a copper can. The temperature rises by 16.3 °C. (a) Calculate the energy transferred to the water. (b) The data-book value is -2021 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest two reasons for the difference. (c) Write the equation for the complete combustion, with state symbols. (d) The thermometer reads to ±0.5 °C. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature rise.
items.answer: (a) 13,600 J (b) Heat loss to surroundings; incomplete combustion; heat absorbed by can; evaporation of fuel. (c) C₃H₇OH(l) + ₄½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l) (d) 6.13%
items.markingKey: (a) 13,600 J [1] (b) Heat loss to surroundings; incomplete combustion; heat absorbed by can; evaporation of fuel. [2] (c) C₃H₇OH(l) + ₄½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l) [2] (d) two readings: ±1.0 °C on ΔT [1]

items.stem: What does Hess's law state?
options: the enthalpy change depends on the route
bond energies are the same in all compounds
the enthalpy change is always negative
the enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final conditions are the same
items.answer: the enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final conditions are the same
items.markingKey: Conservation of energy: ΔH depends only on initial and final states.

items.stem: Explain why Hess’s law is needed to find the enthalpy change for converting anhydrous copper(II) sulfate into hydrated copper(II) sulfate.
items.answer: The reaction cannot be carried out directly in a controlled way and the temperature change cannot be measured; instead ΔH of solution of each solid is measured and combined.
items.markingKey: direct reaction cannot be measured [1]; two dissolving steps combined [1]

items.stem: Explain why ΔHf values are used with the products minus reactants, but ΔHc values with reactants minus products.
items.answer: In a formation cycle, elements are the common starting point (arrows up to both sides); in a combustion cycle, CO₂ and H₂O are the common end point (arrows down from both sides).
items.markingKey: formation cycle from elements [1]; combustion cycle to combustion products [1]

items.stem: Use the standard enthalpy changes of formation (kJ mol⁻¹) HCl(g) −92; NH₃(g) −46; NH₄Cl(s) −314 to calculate the standard enthalpy change for the reaction NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s).
items.answer: −176 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΣΔHf(products) = −314 [1]; ΣΔHf(reactants) = −138 (elements zero) [1]; ΔH = −176 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Use the standard enthalpy changes of formation (kJ mol⁻¹) CO₂(g) −394; H₂O(l) −286; Na₂CO₃(s) −1131; NaHCO₃(s) −951 to calculate the standard enthalpy change for the reaction 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
items.answer: +91 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΣΔHf(products) = −1811 [1]; ΣΔHf(reactants) = −1902 (elements zero) [1]; ΔH = +91 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Use the standard enthalpy changes of formation (kJ mol⁻¹) CO(g) −111; CO₂(g) −394; Fe₂O₃(s) −824 to calculate the standard enthalpy change for the reaction Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g). Draw the energy cycle you used and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: −25 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΣΔHf(products) = −1182 [1]; ΣΔHf(reactants) = −1157 (elements zero) [1]; ΔH = −25 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]; cycle via elements with arrows correct and exothermic [1]

items.stem: In a school laboratory in Nairobi, students find ΔH(solution) of CuSO₄(s) = −66.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and of CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) = +11.7 kJ mol⁻¹, to find the enthalpy change of hydration of the anhydrous salt. (a) Draw an energy cycle linking the two solution enthalpies to the hydration reaction. (b) Explain why this enthalpy change cannot be measured directly.
items.answer: (a) CuSO₄(s) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) (ΔH); both → CuSO₄(aq) via ΔH1 and ΔH2. (b) Water cannot be added in exactly the right amount; hydration is slow/incomplete and the solid’s temperature change cannot be measured.
items.markingKey: (a) CuSO₄(s) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) (ΔH); both → CuSO₄(aq) via ΔH1 and ΔH2. [2] (b) Water cannot be added in exactly the right amount; hydration is slow/incomplete and the solid’s temperature change cannot be measured. [2]

items.stem: Arjun wants the enthalpy change for CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s). The enthalpy change of solution of anhydrous CuSO₄ is −66.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and of CuSO₄·5H₂O is +11.5 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) State Hess's law. (b) Draw an energy cycle linking the two solution enthalpies to the hydration reaction. (c) Calculate the enthalpy change for the hydration of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
items.answer: (a) ΔH is independent of the route, provided initial and final conditions are the same. (b) CuSO₄(s) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) (ΔH); both → CuSO₄(aq) via ΔH1 and ΔH2. (c) −78.0 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) ΔH is independent of the route, provided initial and final conditions are the same. [1] (b) CuSO₄(s) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) (ΔH); both → CuSO₄(aq) via ΔH1 and ΔH2. [2] (c) ΔH = ΔH1 − ΔH2 = −66.5 − (+11.5) [2]

items.stem: Which formula uses enthalpy changes of formation to find ΔHr?
items.answer: ΔHr = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants)
items.markingKey: Route via elements: reactants → elements → products.

items.stem: Explain why the enthalpy change for C(graphite) → C(diamond) is found using combustion data.
items.answer: The conversion cannot be carried out directly under standard conditions; both forms can be burned to CO₂, and the difference gives ΔH.
items.markingKey: cannot be measured directly [1]; both combust to CO₂ [1]

items.stem: A student in Doha claims that δHr = ΣΔHf(reactants) − ΣΔHf(products). Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. It is products minus reactants: ΔHr = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants).
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: In a test answer, Diego states: "The enthalpy change of a reaction is larger if it is carried out in two steps." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Hess’s law: ΔH is the same whatever the route, provided initial and final conditions are the same.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: In a test answer, Nadia states: "The enthalpy change of a reaction is larger if it is carried out in two steps." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Hess’s law: ΔH is the same whatever the route, provided initial and final conditions are the same.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Use the standard enthalpy changes of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹) C₃H₆(g) −2058; C₃H₈(g) −2220; H₂(g) −286 to calculate the enthalpy change for the hydrogenation of propene: C₃H₆(g) + H₂(g) → C₃H₈(g).
items.answer: −124 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΔHr = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products) [1]; correct substitution [1]; −124 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Use the standard enthalpy changes of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹) C₂H₄(g) −1411; C₂H₆(g) −1560; C₄H₁₀(g) −2877 to calculate the enthalpy change for the cracking of butane: C₄H₁₀(g) → C₂H₆(g) + C₂H₄(g).
items.answer: +94 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΔHr = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products) [1]; correct substitution [1]; +94 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Noah wants the enthalpy change for CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s). The enthalpy change of solution of anhydrous CuSO₄ is −66.5 kJ mol⁻¹ and of CuSO₄·5H₂O is +11.5 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) State Hess's law. (b) Calculate the enthalpy change for the hydration of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
items.answer: (a) ΔH is independent of the route, provided initial and final conditions are the same. (b) −78.0 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) ΔH is independent of the route, provided initial and final conditions are the same. [1] (b) ΔH = ΔH1 − ΔH2 = −66.5 − (+11.5) [2]

(a) Draw an energy cycle linking the two solution enthalpies to the hydration reaction. (b) Explain why this enthalpy change cannot be measured directly. items.stem: Which expression gives ΔH using bond energies?
options: Σ(bond energies of bonds broken) − Σ(bond energies of bonds formed)
items.answer: Σ(bond energies of bonds broken) − Σ(bond energies of bonds formed)
items.markingKey: Breaking is endothermic (+), forming is exothermic (−).

items.stem: Explain why the C=O bond energy used for CO₂ (805 kJ mol⁻¹) differs from the average C=O value (740 kJ mol⁻¹).
items.answer: Bond energy depends on the environment of the bond; the C=O bonds in CO₂ are stronger than the average C=O in aldehydes and ketones.
items.markingKey: depends on environment [1]; average vs specific [1]

items.stem: Explain why the enthalpy change for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl calculated from bond energies is close to the experimental value.
items.answer: All species are diatomic gases and the bond energies for H–H, Cl–Cl and H–Cl are exact (not averages) for these molecules.
items.markingKey: gases [1]; bond energies specific to these molecules, not averages [1]

items.stem: Use the average bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) C=C 610, C–C 350, C–H 410, H–H 436 to calculate the enthalpy change for C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g).
items.answer: −124 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Use the average bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) Cl–Cl 244, C–C 350, C–Cl 340, C–H 410, H–Cl 431 to calculate the enthalpy change for C₂H₆(g) + Cl₂(g) → C₂H₅Cl(g) + HCl(g).
items.answer: −117 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: A chemical engineer in Doha estimates the enthalpy change of H₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2HF(g) from the bond energies F–F 158, H–F 562, H–H 436 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the enthalpy change of the reaction. (b) Explain why the calculated value is only approximate.
items.answer: (a) −530 kJ mol⁻¹ (b) Average bond energies used; real bond energies depend on the molecule; non-gaseous states.
items.markingKey: (a) formed 1124; ΔH = 594 − 1124 [2] (b) Average bond energies used; real bond energies depend on the molecule; non-gaseous states. [2]

items.stem: Why is ΔH calculated from average bond energies different from the value found by experiment?
options: the reaction is too fast to measure
bond energies are always measured wrongly
average bond energies are means over many compounds, and the calculation assumes all species are gases
Hess’s law does not apply to bonds
items.answer: average bond energies are means over many compounds, and the calculation assumes all species are gases
items.markingKey: Actual bond energies depend on the molecule; liquids/solids need extra energy terms.

items.stem: "ΔH = bonds formed − bonds broken." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed), since breaking is endothermic and forming is exothermic.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: A student in Dhaka claims that in CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, all four C–H bonds must be included as formed. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Only one C–H bond actually breaks; or, counting all bonds, 4 C–H broken and 3 C–H formed — the three unchanged bonds cancel.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Using bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) C=O (in CO₂) 805, C–C 350, C–H 410, O=O 496, O–H 460, what is ΔH for C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g)?
items.answer: −2050 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: broken 6460 − formed 8510 = −2050 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: Use the average bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) H–H 436, H–I 299, I–I 151 to calculate the enthalpy change for H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g).
items.answer: −11 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: A chemical engineer in Riyadh estimates the enthalpy change of 2CH₃OH(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(g) from the bond energies C=O (in CO₂) 805, C–H 410, C–O 360, O=O 496, O–H 460 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants. (b) Explain why the calculated value is only approximate.
items.answer: (a) 5588 kJ (b) Average bond energies used; real bond energies depend on the molecule; non-gaseous states.
items.markingKey: (a) 5588 kJ [1] (b) Average bond energies used; real bond energies depend on the molecule; non-gaseous states. [2]

items.stem: A chemical engineer in Singapore estimates the enthalpy change of C₂H₆(g) + Cl₂(g) → C₂H₅Cl(g) + HCl(g) from the bond energies Cl–Cl 244, C–C 350, C–Cl 340, C–H 410, H–Cl 431 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Define the term bond energy. (b) Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants. (c) Explain why the calculated value is only approximate.
items.answer: (a) Energy needed to break one mole of a covalent bond in gaseous molecules (average over many compounds). (b) 3054 kJ (c) Average bond energies used; real bond energies depend on the molecule; non-gaseous states.
items.markingKey: (a) Energy needed to break one mole of a covalent bond in gaseous molecules (average over many compounds). [1] (b) 3054 kJ [1] (c) Average bond energies used; real bond energies depend on the molecule; non-gaseous states. [2]

items.stem: What is the standard enthalpy change of formation of an element in its standard state?
options: equal to its enthalpy of atomisation
items.answer: zero
items.markingKey: By definition ΔHf of an element in its standard state is 0.

items.stem: Mei writes in a revision note: "The standard enthalpy change of formation of water is the enthalpy change for 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. ΔHf refers to one mole of product: H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l).
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = +206 kJ mol⁻¹ and an activation energy of 326 kJ mol⁻¹. Sketch a labelled reaction pathway diagram and calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
items.answer: endothermic: products above reactants; Ea(reverse) = 120 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: products above reactants with ΔH labelled [1]; Ea hump labelled from reactants [1]; Ea(reverse) = 326 − (+206) = 120 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: A fuel company in Colombo reports enthalpy data for propane. (a) State the meaning of the term standard conditions. (b) Explain why combustion is exothermic in terms of bonds. (c) Write the equation for the standard enthalpy change of formation of water.
items.answer: (a) 298 K and 101 kPa (solutions 1 mol dm⁻³). (b) Energy released forming bonds in CO₂/H₂O exceeds energy absorbed breaking bonds in fuel and O₂. (c) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l)
items.markingKey: (a) 298 K and 101 kPa (solutions 1 mol dm⁻³). [1] (b) Energy released forming bonds in CO₂/H₂O exceeds energy absorbed breaking bonds in fuel and O₂. [2] (c) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) [1]

items.stem: What is the main source of error in measuring an enthalpy change of combustion using a spirit burner and a copper can?
items.answer: heat loss to the surroundings
items.markingKey: Much heat escapes to the air; also incomplete combustion; so the value is less exothermic than the data book.

items.stem: Kenji writes in a revision note: "In q = mcΔT, m is the mass of fuel burned." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. m is the mass of the water (or solution) being heated.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: A school in Jakarta investigates the energy released by different fuels. (a) Explain why the temperature rise is the same when 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ HCl is neutralised by 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH as when 100 cm³ of each is used. (b) Explain why the experimental enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol is much less exothermic than the data-book value.
items.answer: (a) Twice the amount of water forms, releasing twice the energy, but this heats twice the mass of solution, so ΔT is the same. (b) Heat is lost to the surroundings (air, can); incomplete combustion; evaporation of fuel; non-standard conditions.
items.markingKey: (a) energy doubles; mass doubles, same ΔT [2] (b) heat loss; one other valid reason [2]

items.stem: Zara, a student in Nairobi, mixes 40.0 cm³ of 1.50 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid with 40.0 cm³ of 1.50 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by 10.2 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation. Assume the solution has density 1.00 g cm⁻³ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
items.answer: −56.8 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Isla, a student in Lima, adds an excess of zinc powder to 25.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ copper(II) sulfate solution. The maximum temperature rise, found by extrapolation, is 26.0 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; density 1.00 g cm⁻³)
items.answer: −217 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: In an AS practical class in Mumbai, students heat 200 g of water using 0.90 g of methanol. The water temperature increases by 11.0 °C. (a) The data-book value is -726 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest two reasons for the difference. (b) Suggest two improvements to the experiment. (c) The thermometer reads to ±0.5 °C. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature rise.
items.answer: (a) Heat loss to surroundings; incomplete combustion; heat absorbed by can; evaporation of fuel. (b) Draught shield/insulation; lid; reduce distance from flame; weigh burner with cap on. (c) 9.09%
items.markingKey: (a) Heat loss to surroundings; incomplete combustion; heat absorbed by can; evaporation of fuel. [2] (b) Draught shield/insulation; lid; reduce distance from flame; weigh burner with cap on. [2] (c) two readings: ±1.0 °C on ΔT [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which formula uses enthalpy changes of combustion to find ΔHr? (b) State Hess's law.
items.answer: (a) ΔHr = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products) (b) The total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final conditions are the same.
items.markingKey: (a) Both reactants and products burn to the same CO₂ and H₂O. (b) [1]

items.stem: A student in Lisbon uses Hess’s law to find enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly. Explain why ΔHf values are used with the products minus reactants, but ΔHc values with reactants minus products.
items.answer: In a formation cycle, elements are the common starting point (arrows up to both sides); in a combustion cycle, CO₂ and H₂O are the common end point (arrows down from both sides).
items.markingKey: formation cycle from elements; combustion cycle to combustion products [2]

items.stem: Use the standard enthalpy changes of formation (kJ mol⁻¹) C₃H₆(g) +20; C₃H₈(g) −105 to calculate the standard enthalpy change for the reaction C₃H₈(g) → C₃H₆(g) + H₂(g).
items.answer: +125 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΣΔHf(products) = +20 [1]; ΣΔHf(reactants) = −105 (elements zero) [1]; ΔH = +125 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Use the standard enthalpy changes of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹) C₂H₄(g) −1411; C₂H₅OH(l) −1367 to calculate the enthalpy change for the hydration of ethene: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(l) → C₂H₅OH(l).
items.answer: −44 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΔHr = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products) [1]; correct substitution [1]; −44 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Use the standard enthalpy changes of combustion (kJ mol⁻¹) C(s) −394, H₂(g) −286 and ethane −1560 to calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethane: 2C(s) + 3H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g).
items.answer: −86 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΔHf = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΔHc(product) [1]; = 2(−394) + 3(−286) − (−1560) [1]; = −86 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Amara wants the enthalpy change for CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s). The enthalpy change of solution of anhydrous CuSO₄ is −67.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and of CuSO₄·5H₂O is +12.0 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the enthalpy change for the hydration of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. (b) Explain why this enthalpy change cannot be measured directly. (c) Describe how the enthalpy change of solution of anhydrous CuSO₄ could be measured.
items.answer: (a) −79.0 kJ mol⁻¹ (b) Water cannot be added in exactly the right amount; hydration is slow/incomplete and the solid’s temperature change cannot be measured. (c) Add a weighed mass of solid to a measured volume of water in a polystyrene cup; record the maximum temperature change; q = mcΔT; ΔH = −q/n.
items.markingKey: (a) ΔH = ΔH1 − ΔH2 = −67.0 − (+12.0) [2] (b) Water cannot be added in exactly the right amount; hydration is slow/incomplete and the solid’s temperature change cannot be measured. [2] (c) Add a weighed mass of solid to a measured volume of water in a polystyrene cup; record the maximum temperature change; q = mcΔT; ΔH = −q/n. [2]

items.stem: Ana calculates enthalpy changes using a table of average bond energies. Explain why the enthalpy change for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl calculated from bond energies is close to the experimental value.
items.answer: All species are diatomic gases and the bond energies for H–H, Cl–Cl and H–Cl are exact (not averages) for these molecules.
items.markingKey: gases; bond energies specific to these molecules, not averages [2]

items.stem: "In CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, all four C–H bonds must be included as formed." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Only one C–H bond actually breaks; or, counting all bonds, 4 C–H broken and 3 C–H formed — the three unchanged bonds cancel.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Use the average bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) C=C 610, C–C 350, C–H 410, C–O 360, O–H 460 to calculate the enthalpy change for C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(g).
items.answer: −50 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Samuel uses bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) Cl–Cl 244, C–C 350, C–Cl 340, C–H 410, H–Cl 431 to study the reaction C₂H₆(g) + Cl₂(g) → C₂H₅Cl(g) + HCl(g). (a) Define the term bond energy. (b) Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants. (c) Draw an enthalpy profile showing the bond-breaking and bond-forming steps.
items.answer: (a) Energy needed to break one mole of a covalent bond in gaseous molecules (average over many compounds). (b) 3054 kJ (c) Reactants → gaseous atoms (up by bonds broken) → products (down by bonds formed); net ΔH labelled.
items.markingKey: (a) Energy needed to break one mole of a covalent bond in gaseous molecules (average over many compounds). [1] (b) 3054 kJ [1] (c) Reactants → gaseous atoms (up by bonds broken) → products (down by bonds formed); net ΔH labelled. [2]

items.stem: What is the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation?
options: the enthalpy change when one mole of acid reacts completely
the energy needed to neutralise one mole of base
the enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed by the reaction of an acid with an alkali under standard conditions
the enthalpy change when one mole of salt dissolves
items.answer: the enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed by the reaction of an acid with an alkali under standard conditions
items.markingKey: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), about −57 kJ mol⁻¹ for strong acid + strong base.

items.stem: A student in Lagos is comparing exothermic and endothermic processes. Explain why the enthalpy change of neutralisation of ethanoic acid with NaOH is less exothermic than that of HCl with NaOH.
items.answer: Ethanoic acid is weak and only partly ionised; some energy is used to ionise it as it reacts.
items.markingKey: weak acid partly ionised; energy used for ionisation [2]

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = −286 kJ mol⁻¹ and an activation energy of 120 kJ mol⁻¹. Sketch a labelled reaction pathway diagram and calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
items.answer: exothermic: products below reactants; Ea(reverse) = 406 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: products below reactants with ΔH labelled [1]; Ea hump labelled from reactants [1]; Ea(reverse) = 120 − (−286) = 406 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Tomás is studying the combustion of propane as a fuel for a project in Cairo. (a) Explain why combustion is exothermic in terms of bonds. (b) Sketch a reaction pathway diagram for the combustion, labelling ΔH and Ea.
items.answer: (a) Energy released forming bonds in CO₂/H₂O exceeds energy absorbed breaking bonds in fuel and O₂. (b) Products below reactants; ΔH negative arrow down; Ea from reactants to peak.
items.markingKey: (a) Energy released forming bonds in CO₂/H₂O exceeds energy absorbed breaking bonds in fuel and O₂. [2] (b) Products below reactants; ΔH negative arrow down; Ea from reactants to peak. [2]

items.stem: What mass is used for m when 25.0 cm³ of acid is mixed with 25.0 cm³ of alkali?
items.markingKey: Assume density 1.00 g cm⁻³: total volume 50.0 cm³ → 50.0 g.

items.stem: A school in Mumbai investigates the energy released by different fuels. Suggest two improvements to a spirit-burner experiment to obtain a more accurate value of ΔHc.
items.answer: Use a draught shield/lid; insulate the can; use a copper calorimeter; keep the flame close; put a cap on the burner when weighing; stir the water.
items.markingKey: any two improvements [2]

items.stem: Arjun, a student in Karachi, burns 0.80 g of propan-1-ol, C₃H₇OH, in a spirit burner under a copper can containing 100 g of water. The temperature of the water rises by 38.7 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol in kJ mol⁻¹. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
items.answer: −1210 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which formula uses enthalpy changes of formation to find ΔHr? (b) What is ΔHf of oxygen gas, O₂(g)?
items.answer: (a) ΔHr = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) (b) 0 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) Route via elements: reactants → elements → products. (b) Element in its standard state.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the enthalpy change for C(graphite) → C(diamond) is found using combustion data. (b) Explain why Hess’s law is needed to find the enthalpy change for converting anhydrous copper(II) sulfate into hydrated copper(II) sulfate.
items.answer: (a) The conversion cannot be carried out directly under standard conditions; both forms can be burned to CO₂, and the difference gives ΔH. (b) The reaction cannot be carried out directly in a controlled way and the temperature change cannot be measured; instead ΔH of solution of each solid is measured and combined.
items.markingKey: (a) cannot be measured directly [1]; both combust to CO₂ [1] (b) direct reaction cannot be measured [1]; two dissolving steps combined [1]

items.stem: Use the standard enthalpy changes of formation (kJ mol⁻¹) C₂H₄(g) +52; C₂H₆(g) −85; C₄H₁₀(g) −126 to calculate the standard enthalpy change for the reaction C₄H₁₀(g) → C₂H₆(g) + C₂H₄(g).
items.answer: +93 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΣΔHf(products) = −33 [1]; ΣΔHf(reactants) = −126 (elements zero) [1]; ΔH = +93 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Use the standard enthalpy changes of formation (kJ mol⁻¹) C₂H₅OH(l) −277; CO₂(g) −394; H₂O(l) −286 to calculate the standard enthalpy change for the reaction C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l).
items.answer: −1369 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΣΔHf(products) = −1646 [1]; ΣΔHf(reactants) = −277 (elements zero) [1]; ΔH = −1369 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]

items.answer: (a) ΔH is independent of the route, provided initial and final conditions are the same. (b) −79.0 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Sofia calculates enthalpy changes using a table of average bond energies. Explain why the C=O bond energy used for CO₂ (805 kJ mol⁻¹) differs from the average C=O value (740 kJ mol⁻¹).
items.answer: Bond energy depends on the environment of the bond; the C=O bonds in CO₂ are stronger than the average C=O in aldehydes and ketones.
items.markingKey: depends on environment; average vs specific [2]
